concept.name: Bulkhead & Fault Isolation

relationships.description: Bulkheads limit damage; breakers stop calling failing deps.

reviewRecord.reviewNotes: Seeded for SPEC-062 pillar coverage matrix.

spark.summary: The bulkhead pattern partitions shared compute, thread pools, connection pools, and memory into isolated compartments so a slow or failing downstream dependency exhausts only its own quota rather than sinking the entire service.
spark.keyTakeaway: Timeouts and circuit breakers react after failures happen; bulkheads bound the blast radius structurally before a single slow dependency can starve healthy endpoints.

concept.whyItMatters: In a shared-pool architecture (e.g., a 200-thread Tomcat/Jetty server calling three downstream APIs), a single stalled dependency with a 30-second timeout will capture all 200 threads within seconds. Healthy endpoints like `/healthz`, login, or catalog browse freeze completely—turning a minor partial degradation into a total cascading outage.
whenToUse: Services calling multiple downstream dependencies with different SLAs (e.g., critical payment gateway vs. non-critical recommendations or analytics).
Multi-tenant SaaS platforms where a noisy neighbor's bursty queries or large exports could starve CPU, DB connections, or queue workers for other tenants.
Mixed latency workloads (fast 10ms cache lookups sharing a process with 2-second PDF generation or LLM inference calls).
whenNotToUse: Strictly single-purpose microservices with only one downstream dependency—a circuit breaker and tight timeout suffice without internal pool fragmentation.
Extreme memory-constrained environments where dozens of tiny static thread pools waste stack memory (1 MB/thread in JVM) and sit mostly idle.
When dynamic, fair-share scheduling (e.g., weighted fair queuing at an async event loop) already prevents head-of-line blocking without hard static caps.
keyPoints: Size pools using Little's Law ($L = \lambda \times W$): a dependency handling 400 RPS at 50ms average latency needs ~20 concurrent slots, plus a small burst buffer (e.g., 30 max).

Thread-pool bulkheads (Resilience4j `ThreadPoolBulkhead`) provide true timeout interruption and isolation; semaphore bulkheads (`SemaphoreBulkhead`, Envoy `max_requests`) have near-zero overhead but cannot interrupt blocking I/O.
Database connection pools (HikariCP) should be partitioned by workload criticality (e.g., OLTP checkout pool vs. reporting/backfill pool) or routed via separate PgBouncer pools.

Infrastructure-level bulkheads—Linux cgroups v2 (`cpu.max`, `memory.max`), Kubernetes `ResourceQuota` + separate Deployments, and Envoy per-cluster circuit breakers—isolate failures across processes and tenants.
Always pair bulkheads with a fast-fail `maxWaitDuration` (e.g., 0–25ms) and graceful degradation (cached fallback or HTTP 429/503) rather than unbounded request queuing.

examples.title: E-Commerce API Gateway Isolating Slow Loyalty Service
examples.scenario: An order-details BFF aggregates Inventory (15ms p99), Pricing (20ms p99), and Loyalty Points (normally 40ms, but degrades to 15s during a batch job) inside a 200-thread Spring Boot service.
examples.outcome: Wrapping the Loyalty client in a Resilience4j `ThreadPoolBulkhead` (`coreThreadPoolSize=15`, `maxThreadPoolSize=25`, `queueCapacity=10`) caps Loyalty's footprint at 25 threads. When Loyalty stalls, checkout and pricing stay at 99.99% availability while Loyalty sections gracefully fall back to 'Points updating shortly'.

examples.title: Multi-Tenant Postgres Connection Pool Partitioning
examples.scenario: A SaaS analytics app shares one 100-connection HikariCP pool across interactive dashboard queries (20ms) and CSV export jobs (12s). Three concurrent exports exhaust connections and freeze all user logins.
examples.outcome: Splitting into `oltp-pool` (70 connections, 2s statement timeout) and `export-pool` (15 connections, dedicated worker Deployment) completely eliminates login timeouts during peak export hours.

tradeOffs.pro: Hard per-dependency caps guarantee that a stalled integration cannot consume 100% of threads, sockets, or memory.
tradeOffs.con: Static partitions reduce statistical multiplexing—idle threads in the Payments bulkhead cannot help a sudden spike in Search traffic.

tradeOffs.pro: Thread pools isolate blocking calls and enforce caller-side timeouts; semaphores add <1 microsecond overhead with zero context-switching.
tradeOffs.con: Thread pools add context-switch overhead and 1 MB/thread stack memory; semaphores leave the caller thread blocked until the socket times out.

tradeOffs.pro: A small bounded queue absorbs micro-bursts (e.g., 10–20ms GC pauses) without dropping requests.
tradeOffs.con: Deep queues mask overload, inflate p99 latency, and waste CPU processing requests whose clients have already timed out.

failureModes.name: Unbounded Bulkhead Queue Causes OOM
failureModes.description: Configuring a thread-pool bulkhead with an unbounded `LinkedBlockingQueue` lets stalled requests pile up in heap until the JVM crashes with `OutOfMemoryError`.
failureModes.mitigation: Always set a tight, bounded `queueCapacity` (e.g., 10–50) or `0` (`SynchronousQueue`) and reject excess with HTTP 503.

failureModes.name: Hidden Shared Bottleneck Beneath Separate Pools
failureModes.description: Two services have separate thread pools, yet both write to the same Redis single-threaded instance or shared NAT gateway port pool, re-creating a single point of failure.
failureModes.mitigation: Audit the full dependency graph (CPU, NIC, NAT ports, DNS resolver, DB locks) and isolate shared downstream quotas too.

failureModes.name: Under-Sized Bulkhead Triggers False Rejections
failureModes.description: Sizing a pool for average latency without accounting for p99 bursts causes healthy traffic spikes to hit `BulkheadFullException` prematurely.
failureModes.mitigation: Calculate size from peak RPS $\times$ p99 latency + 25% headroom, and monitor `resilience4j.bulkhead.available.concurrent.calls`.

failureModes.name: Retry Storm Amplifies Bulkhead Saturation
failureModes.description: Upstream callers immediately retry 503s from a full bulkhead 3x, multiplying inbound concurrency by 4x and keeping the compartment pinned.
failureModes.mitigation: Return `Retry-After` headers, use exponential backoff with full jitter, and enforce client-side retry budgets (max 10–20% retry ratio).

commonMistakes: Using `SemaphoreBulkhead` around blocking HTTP clients that lack aggressive socket read timeouts, leaving caller threads stuck anyway.
Setting thread-pool queue sizes to 1,000+ instead of failing fast when concurrency exceeds healthy limits.
Isolating application threads while leaving a single shared HikariCP database pool or shared Kafka consumer group.
Forgetting to propagate tracing context (`MDC` / OpenTelemetry `Context`) across `ThreadPoolBulkhead` worker threads.
Never load-testing partial-failure scenarios (e.g., injecting 10s latency via Toxiproxy) to verify bulkhead caps actually hold.

sections.content:
## The idea

Named after watertight compartments in a ship's hull, the **bulkhead pattern** divides a system's finite resources—worker threads, DB connections, memory, CPU cores, or tenant shards—into bounded, independent pools. If one downstream dependency hangs or one tenant triggers a heavy workload, only its assigned compartment fills up and sheds load. Unrelated features and healthy tenants continue operating at full speed with their own untouched resource quotas.

## Concrete walkthrough

Suppose an API server runs 200 worker threads and serves `/checkout` (calls Payments, 40ms p95) and `/recommendations` (calls ML Ranker, 30ms p95).

1. **Without Bulkheads**: ML Ranker's vector DB locks up and requests hang until the 10-second socket timeout. At 100 RPS, all 200 server threads are blocked waiting on ML Ranker within 2 seconds. `/checkout` and `/healthz` stop responding, and the load balancer marks the entire node unhealthy.
2. **With Bulkheads**: You partition outbound concurrency using Little's Law:
   - **Payments Bulkhead**: 60 max concurrent calls, `maxWaitDuration = 20ms`.
   - **ML Ranker Bulkhead**: 25 max concurrent calls, `queueCapacity = 0`, `maxWaitDuration = 0ms`.
3. **Under Failure**: When ML Ranker hangs, its 25 slots fill in 250ms. The 26th request fails immediately in <1ms with `BulkheadFullException`, returning a cached top-sellers fallback. Meanwhile, 175 threads remain free for `/checkout` and `/healthz`.

sections.content:
## Sizing pools with Little's Law

Guessing pool sizes leads to either starvation or wasted memory. Use **Little's Law** ($L = \lambda \times W$) where $L$ is required concurrency, $\lambda$ is peak arrival rate (RPS), and $W$ is target response time in seconds. For 500 RPS at 40ms (0.04s) p95 latency, $L = 500 \times 0.04 = 20$ concurrent slots. Add 25%–50% burst headroom (25–30 slots) so normal variance does not shed load, and pair with a circuit breaker that opens if failure rate exceeds 50% over a 10-second sliding window.

## Isolation mechanisms compared

| Mechanism | Layer | Memory / CPU Overhead | Can Interrupt Blocked I/O? | Best Fit |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Semaphore (`SemaphoreBulkhead`)** | In-process | ~100 ns (atomic counter) | No (caller thread waits) | Non-blocking async/WebFlux or fast-timeout calls |
| **Thread Pool (`ThreadPoolBulkhead`)** | In-process | ~1 MB stack/thread + switch | Yes (`Future.cancel`) | Blocking JDBC/HTTP clients needing strict isolation |
| **Envoy `max_requests` / `max_pending`** | Sidecar / Mesh | Low (event-loop counters) | Yes (resets upstream stream) | Polyglot microservices on Kubernetes / Istio |
| **Separate Deployment + `cgroups`** | Process / Node | Highest (duplicate pods) | Yes (OS process boundary) | Noisy-neighbor multi-tenancy, heavy batch vs OLTP |

## Failure modes

1. **Queue Bloat**: A bulkhead with `queueCapacity = 500` turns fast-fail into a 500-request latency trap where every caller times out before its queued task even starts.
2. **Shared Resource Leakage**: Isolating HTTP threads while sharing one DNS resolver (`systemd-resolved`), one NAT gateway ephemeral port table, or one HikariCP pool still allows cascading failure.
3. **Retry Amplification**: Without retry budgets (e.g., Envoy `retry_budget: 20%`), clients retrying bulkhead 503s multiply load during recovery.

sections.eyebrow: 06 / Combining bulkheads with circuit breakers and shuffle sharding
sections.content:
## Combining bulkheads with circuit breakers and shuffle sharding

Bulkheads, circuit breakers, and **shuffle sharding** form a layered defense. A bulkhead caps max concurrency ($25$ slots); a circuit breaker trips open once those 25 slots consistently fail, dropping wait time from `timeout` to `0ms`. For multi-tenant platforms, **shuffle sharding** (e.g., assigning each tenant 2 virtual workers out of a 10-worker fleet, giving $\binom{10}{2} = 45$ unique combinations) ensures a single toxic tenant can only impact a tiny fraction of other tenants.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Classify all downstream calls and tenant tiers into Critical, Standard, and Best-Effort.
- [ ] Size each bulkhead using Little's Law ($\text{Peak RPS} \times \text{p95 Latency} \times 1.3$).
- [ ] Set `queueCapacity` small (0–25) and `maxWaitDuration` <= 25ms so overload fails fast.
- [ ] Partition database connection pools (HikariCP/PgBouncer) separately from HTTP worker pools.
- [ ] Propagate OpenTelemetry trace/MDC context when using `ThreadPoolBulkhead`.
- [ ] Verify isolation in staging by injecting 10s latency on one dependency via Chaos Mesh or Toxiproxy.

interviewProblems.title: Bulkhead & Fault Isolation
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on Bulkhead & Fault Isolation. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

simulation.title: Interactive Simulation: Bulkhead And Fault Isolation

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: The bulkhead pattern partitions shared compute, thread pools, connection pools, and memory into isolated compartments so a slow or failing downstream dependency exhausts only its own quota rather than sinking the entire service.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: ML Ranker Bulkhead applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Degraded Fallback.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Degraded Fallback experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Always set a tight, bounded `queueCapacity` (e.g., 10–50) or `0` (`SynchronousQueue`) and reject excess with HTTP 503.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Timeouts and circuit breakers react after failures happen; bulkheads bound the blast radius structurally before a single slow dependency can starve healthy endpoints.
Avoid trap: Using `SemaphoreBulkhead` around blocking HTTP clients that lack aggressive socket read timeouts, leaving caller threads stuck anyway.
Avoid trap: Setting thread-pool queue sizes to 1,000+ instead of failing fast when concurrency exceeds healthy limits.
When to reach for it: Services calling multiple downstream dependencies with different SLAs (e.g., critical payment gateway vs. non-critical recommendations or analytics).
When to reach for it: Multi-tenant SaaS platforms where a noisy neighbor's bursty queries or large exports could starve CPU, DB connections, or queue workers for other tenants.

putItTogether.title: Putting Bulkhead And Fault Isolation Together
putItTogether.summary: Timeouts and circuit breakers react after failures happen; bulkheads bound the blast radius structurally before a single slow dependency can starve healthy endpoints.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Bulkhead And Fault Isolation before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Wrapping the Loyalty client in a Resilience4j `ThreadPoolBulkhead` (`coreThreadPoolSize=15`, `maxThreadPoolSize=25`, `queueCapacity=10`) caps Loyalty's footprint at 25 threads. When Loyalty stalls, checkout and pricing stay at 99.99% availability while Loyalty sections gracefully fall back to 'Points updating shortly'.
